main.title: Windjammers
main.subtitle: A flying disc across the court
main.summary: Windjammers is Data East's arcade sports game, first released for Neo Geo on 17 February 1994.

cards.heading: A flying disc across the court
cards.text: Windjammers is Data East's arcade sports game, first released for Neo Geo on 17 February 1994. Two opponents throw a flying disc across a divided court, trying to drive it into the goal behind the other player. Six competitors provide different combinations of speed, strength and special throws. The basic exchange is immediately legible: catch the disc, choose an angle and send it back. As the rally accelerates, that small sequence becomes a rapid contest of positioning, anticipation and the ability to recover before the next return reaches the goal.

cards.heading: The catch becomes the next attack
cards.text: Defence requires meeting the disc or diving to intercept it. Once caught, the player has only a short time to release it and cannot move while holding it, making the choice of return urgent. A throw can travel directly towards a goal or bounce from the side walls. Lofted discs display a landing target that must be reached to prevent a miss. The game keeps changing the shape of the exchange, asking the player to read a fast horizontal shot differently from an airborne disc falling into the court.

cards.heading: Different courts, different openings
cards.text: Goal sections award different points, while missing an airborne disc gives the opponent a smaller score. Each court changes the arrangement of those targets, making the arena itself part of choosing an attacking angle. Barriers can further alter a ricochet. Seiichi Hamada and Tomoyoshi Sato composed the music for the original release. Later adaptations introduced the game to new competitive audiences, and Dotemu eventually developed a sequel. The enduring attraction remains the original's compact chain of decisions, where a successful defensive catch instantly becomes the next chance to score.

main.title: Wario's Woods
main.summary: Wario's Woods, known in Japan as Wario's Forest, is a 1994 puzzle video game developed by Nintendo R&D1 and Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) and Super Nintendo Entertainment System (Super NES).

cards.heading: Toad clears the woods
cards.text: Wario's Woods, known in Japan as Wario's Forest, is a 1994 puzzle video game developed by Nintendo R&D1 and Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) and Super Nintendo Entertainment System (Super NES). A spin-off of the Mario series, players control Toad in his mission to defeat Wario, who has taken control of the Peaceful Woods. Gameplay revolves around clearing each level by using bombs to destroy groups of enemies. The game also features a multiplayer mode that allows two players to compete against each other.

cards.heading: A final North American NES release
cards.text: The NES version is noteworthy for being the last officially-licensed game as well as the final first-party game for the system in North America, due to its release at the end of the console's lifespan. It is also the only NES game to receive a rating from the Entertainment Software Rating Board (ESRB), which was established almost three months before the game's American release. In Japan, the game was released alongside a re-release of The Legend of Zelda to coincide with the release of the AV Famicom.

cards.heading: Ports, reception and a longer life
cards.text: Wario's Woods has been re-released several times for other platforms, such as the Satellaview and the Virtual Console. The game received mixed reviews from critics, who praised its gameplay, design, and multiplayer mode, though some believed it was not as refined as Nintendo's previous puzzle games like Dr. Mario, and lacked depth and enough content to keep players engaged. It was released for the Nintendo Switch as a part of the Nintendo Classics service.

main.title: Super Street Fighter II Turbo
main.summary: Super Street Fighter II Turbo, released in Japan as Super Street Fighter II X: Grand Master Challenge, is a 1994 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades.

cards.heading: Super Street Fighter II Turbo
cards.text: Super Street Fighter II Turbo, released in Japan as Super Street Fighter II X: Grand Master Challenge, is a 1994 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades. It is the fifth and final installment in the Street Fighter II sub-series of Street Fighter games, following Super Street Fighter II (1993). Like its predecessor, it ran on the CP System II hardware.

cards.heading: Super combos and a hidden Akuma
cards.text: Super Turbo introduced new gameplay mechanics, including the addition of combination moves called super combos and air combos. It also introduced the secret character Akuma, who would go on to become a recurring character in later Street Fighter installments and other Capcom fighting games.

cards.heading: Super Street Fighter II Turbo
cards.text: The game was published for 3DO the same year followed by versions for MS-DOS and Amiga. In 1997, conversions were released for PlayStation and Saturn as part of the Street Fighter Collection, and in 2000 for the Dreamcast in as Super Street Fighter II X for Matching Service. A Game Boy Advance version was also made.

cards.heading: Reception and legacy
cards.text: While not as commercially successful as previous iterations of Street Fighter II, Super Turbo was well-received by critics and had a major impact on the competitive fighting game community. Super Street Fighter II Turbo still has an active tournament scene to this day, being one of the most popular retro fighting games in modern day tournaments. A remake was published in 2008 for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360: Super Street Fighter II Turbo HD Remix.

main.title: X-COM: UFO Defense
main.subtitle: Defending Earth, one decision at a time
main.summary: Mythos Games and MicroProse combine global management with turn-based missions in the 1994 X-COM: UFO Defense.

cards.heading: X-COM: defending Earth
cards.text: UFO: Enemy Unknown (original title), also known as X-COM: UFO Defense in North America, is a 1994 science fiction strategy video game developed by Mythos Games and MicroProse. It was published by MicroProse for DOS and Amiga computers, the Amiga CD32 console, and the PlayStation. Originally planned by Julian Gollop as a sequel to Mythos Games' 1988 Laser Squad, the game mixes real-time management simulation with turn-based tactics. The player takes the role of commander of X-COM – an international paramilitary and scientific organisation secretly defending Earth from an alien invasion. Through the game, the player is tasked with issuing orders to individual X-COM troops in a series of turn-based tactical missions. At strategic scale, the player directs the research and development of new technologies, builds and expands X-COM's bases, manages the organisation's finances and personnel, and monitors and responds to UFO activity.

cards.heading: Directing the Geoscape
cards.text: The game begins on 1 January, 1999, with the player choosing a location for their first base on the Geoscape screen: a global view representation of Earth as seen from space (displaying X-COM bases and aircraft, detected UFOs, alien bases, and sites of alien activity). The player can view the X-COM bases and make changes to them, equip fighter aircraft, order supplies and personnel (soldiers, scientists and engineers), direct research efforts, schedule manufacturing of advanced equipment, sell alien artefacts on black market to raise money, and deploy X-COM aircraft to either patrol designated locations, intercept UFOs, or send X-COM ground troops on missions using transport aircraft.

cards.heading: Spending Time Units
cards.text: Each soldier has a number of Time Units determined by their statistics, equipment weight and stamina. Movement, aiming, firing, reloading, kneeling and handling equipment spend those units. Shots can be quick, aimed or automatic when the weapon supports it. Leaving enough units unspent allows Opportunity Fire: a soldier can shoot at a hostile spotted during the enemy's turn.

cards.heading: Research and funding
cards.text: Recovered alien artefacts can be researched and reproduced. Capturing live aliens may reveal further information and technologies, including the possibility of training soldiers in psionic abilities. Meanwhile, the sixteen founding nations review X-COM's progress each month and can increase or reduce its funding. A country infiltrated by the invaders may withdraw its support altogether.

main.title: Streets of Rage 3
main.subtitle: Back on the streets
main.summary: Streets of Rage 3 is Sega's side-scrolling fighting game for Mega Drive, first released in Japan on 18 March 1994 as Bare Knuckle III.

cards.heading: Back on the streets
cards.text: Streets of Rage 3 is Sega's side-scrolling fighting game for Mega Drive, first released in Japan on 18 March 1994 as Bare Knuckle III. Axel, Blaze and Skate return alongside Dr. Zan, a scientist with a mechanical body. Their investigation brings them into another scheme involving Mr. X and robotic replacements for public figures. One or two players fight through streets and buildings, clearing groups of attackers before moving onwards. The familiar procession of punches, throws and improvised weapons now gives the fighters more ways to keep moving.

cards.heading: Keeping the fight moving
cards.text: Every character can run and roll vertically across the screen. These movements help close a gap, escape a surrounding group or approach an enemy from another line. Special attacks draw on a rechargeable meter: using one when the meter is full avoids the usual health cost. Waiting for that opportunity makes the attack a resource to manage during a crowded fight. Weapons wear out through use, while Zan changes the way found weapons behave by converting them into energy attacks suited to his mechanical body.

cards.heading: A changing investigation
cards.text: The journey can reach different endings depending on decisions and performance during the later stages. That gives the rescue and pursuit a consequence beyond reaching the next boss. The Japanese and Western editions also differ in presentation, story details and difficulty, so the same title can recall rather different experiences. Yuzo Koshiro and Motohiro Kawashima returned to compose the soundtrack. Their increasingly experimental electronic music accompanies a sequel whose faster movement and expanded combat push the series further than its outwardly familiar streets first suggest.

main.title: Super Metroid
main.summary: Super Metroid is a 1994 action-adventure game developed by Nintendo and Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).

cards.heading: Returning to Zebes
cards.text: Super Metroid is a 1994 action-adventure game developed by Nintendo and Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). It is the third Metroid game, following the Game Boy game Metroid II: Return of Samus (1991). The player controls bounty hunter Samus Aran, who travels to the planet Zebes to retrieve an infant Metroid creature stolen by the Space Pirate leader Ridley.

cards.heading: New tools change the routes through the world
cards.text: Like the previous two Metroid games, Super Metroid focuses on exploring a sprawling alien world to find power-ups used to reach previously inaccessible areas. New elements include an inventory screen, an automap, and the ability to fire in 8 directions. The development staff from previous Metroid games—including Yoshio Sakamoto, Makoto Kano and Gunpei Yokoi—returned to develop Super Metroid over the course of two years.

cards.heading: A vocabulary for exploration games
cards.text: Super Metroid received acclaim, with praise for its atmosphere, gameplay, music and graphics. It is often cited as one of the greatest video games of all time. The game sold well and shipped 1.42 million copies worldwide by late 2003. Alongside Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, Super Metroid is credited for establishing the Metroidvania genre, inspiring numerous indie games and developers. Super Metroid was followed in 2002 by Metroid Fusion and Metroid Prime. It has been re-released on several Nintendo consoles and services.

main.title: Monster World IV
main.subtitle: An adventure built for two companions
main.summary: Westone’s Monster World IV first appeared on the Japanese Mega Drive on April 1, 1994. Its new heroine Asha sets out into a world with an Arabian Nights flavour, armed with a sword and shield. Towns and shops connect the expedition to side-scrolling stages filled with enemies and environmental obstacles. Her partnership with the mysterious Pepelogoo shapes the adventure. Their expressive movements make that relationship visible during play.

cards.heading: Asha answers the call
cards.text: Westone’s Monster World IV first appeared on the Japanese Mega Drive on April 1, 1994. Its new heroine Asha sets out into a world with an Arabian Nights flavour, armed with a sword and shield. Towns and shops connect the expedition to side-scrolling stages filled with enemies and environmental obstacles. Her partnership with the mysterious Pepelogoo shapes the adventure. Their expressive movements make that relationship visible during play.

cards.heading: A companion changes the platform game
cards.text: Pepelogoo can be called, carried and thrown, helping Asha reach places she could not access alone. The original manual illustrates the creature acting as a platform, as well as Asha holding it above her head. These interactions sit alongside running, directional sword attacks and managing equipment rather than replacing the adventure’s action. Jin Watanabe’s music accompanies the changing locations.

main.title: Final Fantasy VI
main.subtitle: An empire powered by recovered magic
main.summary: Final Fantasy VI begins with an empire turning recovered magic into military power, and people trying to resist it.

cards.heading: An industrial world and an older power
cards.text: Final Fantasy VI begins with an empire turning recovered magic into military power, and people trying to resist it. Square released the Super Famicom game in Japan on 2 April 1994. Its world has rebuilt itself with steam and machinery, but an older destructive force has returned.

cards.heading: People with reasons to resist
cards.text: Terra, called Tina in the Japanese version, has been controlled and used as an imperial weapon. Escape brings her into contact with the Returners. Their allies have different reasons to fight: Locke carries the memory of someone he could not protect, while Edgar balances the safety of his kingdom against opposition to the empire.

cards.heading: After catastrophe
cards.text: That shared struggle does not guarantee that the world can be preserved. Kefka brings catastrophe rather than a defeat neatly contained at the end of a quest. The story follows people whose losses matter beyond the immediate battle. A large fantasy conflict is held together by smaller questions about family, loyalty and a reason to continue.

cards.heading: Equipping weapons, armor and Relics
cards.text: Characters in Final Fantasy VI can be equipped with a variety of weapons, armor and, particular to this entry, powerful accessories known as "Relics". Weapons and armor increase combat capability, mostly by increasing statistics and adding beneficial effects to attacks. By comparison, Relics have a variety of uses and effects, are almost entirely interchangeable among party members, and are extended in sophistication to alter basic battle commands and exceed normal limitations of the game's systems.

cards.heading: The words have a physical limit
cards.text: In a 1994 interview, Ted Woolsey describes translating text that had to fit inside an existing game. Enlarging dialogue windows helped only so far. Shortening a sentence could disturb information needed later in the plot, while messages arrived without a convenient reading order. His example is Secret of Mana, whose scattered text made following the story difficult. The work required remembering connections that the translation files did not display together. A clear English line still had to function at its particular place in the program.

cards.heading: Choosing what crosses the border
cards.text: Woolsey also discussed selecting games for American and European release. He expected to visit Square in Japan and examine projects in development, describing a growing role for the overseas office. His account included plans for Final Fantasy V. Localization involved decisions about which games to release and which audiences to address, alongside the work of translating the chosen projects.

cards.heading: A story delivered in pieces
cards.text: Looking back in 2007, Woolsey described the Super Nintendo game Americans knew as Final Fantasy III: the Japanese Final Fantasy VI. He received a cartridge, files and some unfinished strategy-guide material. The text was divided among many separate files instead of being arranged as a continuous script. He had requested a complete set of videotapes, but recalled that they never arrived.

cards.heading: Rewriting around the same actions
cards.text: His first English delivery was too large, and another shortening pass still failed to fit. Woolsey recalled finally reworking individual sections while preserving their information and the timing of scripted actions. A small team in Japan adjusted memory allocation and other parts of the localized version. Only after the text fitted could he see a playable build containing it.

main.title: Tempest 2000
main.subtitle: A neon edge above the void
main.summary: Tempest 2000 is Jeff Minter's reworking of Atari's 1981 arcade shooter, first released for the Jaguar on 13 April 1994.

cards.heading: A neon edge above the void
cards.text: Tempest 2000 is Jeff Minter's reworking of Atari's 1981 arcade shooter, first released for the Jaguar on 13 April 1994. The player moves a claw-shaped Blaster around the rim of a geometric web, firing down its lanes at enemies climbing towards the edge. It preserves the original's spatial challenge while surrounding it with new effects, electronic music and power-ups. The action remains a matter of choosing the right lane at the right moment as the empty space below becomes increasingly crowded.

cards.heading: Power-ups on a changing web
cards.text: The campaign crosses one hundred webs with changing shapes, colors and enemy arrangements. Power-ups add abilities and rewards to the familiar circuit around the rim, while bonus sections interrupt the shooting with another kind of movement. New enemy types change the danger attached to each lane. The player has to read the whole web while reacting to the nearest threat, often moving past a promising target to stop something closer to the edge. Success unlocks a harder Beastly Mode, extending the challenge beyond the first complete run.

cards.heading: Minter turns the arcade inside out
cards.text: Developed by Llamasoft, the Jaguar version made Minter's interest in visual intensity and arcade scoring especially visible. Alastair Lindsay, Ian Howe and Kevin Saville supplied the soundtrack, giving the abstract battle a strong musical identity. Particles and bright colors amplify a design whose geometry remains essential to understanding the action. Later versions reached computers, Saturn and PlayStation, with changes between them. The original Jaguar release became one of the console's defining games through the close connection between its old arcade foundation and its exuberant presentation.

main.title: Ridge Racer 2
main.summary: Ridge Racer 2 is a 1994 racing video game developed and published by Namco for arcades.

cards.heading: A sequel built around linked racing
cards.text: Ridge Racer 2 is a 1994 racing video game developed and published by Namco for arcades. A sequel to Ridge Racer, it features more quality-of-life changes than substantial new content. One major addition is the ability to play with up to eight human players.

cards.heading: From Rave Racer to Revolution
cards.text: The game would be followed up by Rave Racer. The PlayStation version of Ridge Racer was followed up by Ridge Racer Revolution, which inherited Ridge Racer 2's soundtrack.

cards.heading: Eight drivers link their cabinets
cards.text: The gameplay is very much like that of the original, but unlike the vanilla version of Ridge Racer (which was a single-player game), in Ridge Racer 2 up to eight players can play simultaneously when four two-player cabinets are linked together. A player's number determines their car.

cards.heading: New music, mirrors and nightfall
cards.text: There also are six new songs, including remixed ones from the original, that can be selected with the gear shifter at the start. The enormous television screen above the entrance to the first tunnel shows footage from Namco's 1979 title Galaxian (in the original, it was playing Mappy). There is a rear-view mirror at the top of the screen, so a player can see other cars coming from behind. There is also a change in daylight from day to night (a car driven into the track's tunnel during the day will come out the other end at night).

cards.heading: Fourth in the arcade charts
cards.text: In Japan, Game Machine listed Ridge Racer 2 on their August 15, 1994 issue as being the fourth most-successful upright/cockpit arcade game of the month. In North America, RePlay reported the game to be the fourth most-popular deluxe arcade game at the time. Play Meter also listed the title to be the thirty-seventh most-popular arcade game at the time.

cards.heading: Arcade rivalry through linked multiplayer
cards.text: Next Generation reviewed the arcade version of the game, rating it four stars out of five, and stated that "eight-user multi-player link-up has been added to enable Ridge Racer 2 to compete on equal footing with Sega's Daytona USA and Namco's new Ace Driver." In 2023, Time Extension ranked the game 11th on their "Best Ridge Racer Games" list.
